claims.claim: The first Oxford penicillin patient (policeman Albert Alexander, February 1941) improved on penicillin, and the drug was recovered from his urine for re-use, but the supply was insufficient and he relapsed and died.
claims.episode_span: In February 1941 a single patient in Oxford received nearly all the penicillin the research team could make
claims.supporting_quote: However, the researchers did not have enough penicillin to help him to a full recovery. Penicillin was recovered from his urine, but it was not enough.

claims.claim: Deep-tank submerged fermentation replaced shallow surface culture; Pfizer converted a Brooklyn ice plant into the first deep-submergence production plant with fourteen 130,000-litre stirred tanks.
claims.episode_span: Deep-tank submerged fermentation replaced the flasks with sealed, stirred, aerated vessels of thousands of liters.
claims.supporting_quote: converted into the first deep-submergence production plant, with fourteen 130,000-litre (34,000 US gal) tanks.

claims.claim: The higher-yielding production strain came from a cantaloupe bought at a Peoria fruit market, identified as Penicillium chrysogenum (NRRL 1951).
claims.episode_span: The second move replaced the original low-yielding strain with isolates from a moldy cantaloupe collected in Peoria
claims.supporting_quote: The best sample, however, was from a cantaloupe sold in a Peoria fruit market in 1943. The mould was identified as Penicillium chrysogenum

claims.claim: Corn steep liquor, a cheap byproduct of the corn wet-milling industry, increased penicillin yields roughly tenfold when added to the growth medium.
claims.episode_span: corn steep liquor, a cheap by-product of wet-milling, supplied nitrogen and growth factors at commodity prices on the order of a few cents per kilogram
claims.supporting_quote: An even larger increase occurred when Moyer added corn steep liquor , a byproduct of the corn industry that the NRRL routinely tried in the hope of finding more uses for it. The effect on penicillin was dramatic; Heatley and Moyer found that it increased the yield tenfold.

claims.claim: US penicillin production rose from 21 billion Oxford units in 1943 to about 1,663 billion units in 1944 and an estimated 6,852 billion units in 1945.
claims.episode_span: Published wartime production figures show output rising from kilograms per month to tons per month within roughly two years.
claims.supporting_quote: US penicillin production rose from 21 billion units in 1943, to 1,663 billion units in 1944 and an estimated 6,852

claims.claim: By D-Day (June 6, 1944) the Allied invasion force was supplied with millions of doses of penicillin.
claims.episode_span: Three years later, on the beaches of Normandy, medical units carried enough penicillin to treat every wounded soldier who needed it.
claims.source_title: D-Day invasion was bolstered by UW-Madison penicillin project (news.wisc.edu)
claims.supporting_quote: On June 6, 1944, the D-Day invasion of Normandy was bolstered by millions of doses of a precious new substance: penicillin.

claims.claim: By the end of WWII the cost of 100,000 units of penicillin had fallen from about $20 to three cents.
claims.episode_span: The Idiot Index of the process fell sharply because the dominant costs shifted from repetitive small-scale handling to the capital cost of tanks and compressors, which could then be amortized over far larger volumes.
claims.source_title: D-Day invasion was bolstered by UW-Madison penicillin project (news.wisc.edu)
claims.supporting_quote: By the end of the war, the cost of 100,000 units of penicillin — just a fraction of a single dose — dropped from $20 (about $500 today) to three cents.

claims.claim: Penicillin was first given to a human on 12 February 1941 at Oxford's Radcliffe Infirmary (policeman Albert Alexander); because supply was so low the drug was extracted from his urine and re-injected, and the supply ran out before he could be cured.
claims.episode_span: when the drug appeared in his urine it was collected, purified again, and given back to him because there was nothing else
claims.source_title: On this site: Penicillin - a historic first | Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences, University of Oxford
claims.supporting_quote: However, due to the low supply of the new drug, the penicillin had to be extracted from Mr Alexander’s urine and re-injected. Unfortunately the supply ran out before he could be cured and he later died on 14 March 1941.

claims.claim: Under Oxford's 1941 surface-culture method, about 2,000 litres of culture fluid were needed to obtain enough penicillin to treat a single case of sepsis; recovered drug from patients' urine was reused (a vial dated 25 June 1941 survives).
claims.episode_span: so oxygen reached the mold slowly and yields stayed low, often measured in a few milligrams per liter
claims.source_title: Original penicillin culture and specimen | History of Science Museum, University of Oxford
claims.supporting_quote: 2000 litres of culture fluid were required to obtain enough penicillin to treat a single case of sepsis. The team therefore worked hard to increase the yield from the cultures.

claims.claim: The high-yielding production strain (Penicillium NRRL 1951) was found growing on a cantaloupe at a Peoria market near the USDA laboratory, and grown in vats of corn-steep liquor it produced more penicillin than Fleming's original strain.
claims.episode_span: The second move replaced the original low-yielding strain with isolates from a moldy cantaloupe collected in Peoria
claims.source_title: Penicillium Strain Named State Microbe of Illinois : USDA ARS
claims.supporting_quote: Ironically, the mold strain was discovered growing on a cantaloupe at the local market, not far from the laboratory. The scientists' studies showed that when grown in vats of corn-steep liquor and other nutrients, the mold churned out more penicillin than the Penicillium strain originally discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.

claims.claim: Fleming's original strain, brought to Peoria by Oxford scientists in 1941, yielded too little under the submerged-culture conditions industry needed; the Peoria strain (PS46 / NRRL 1951) was the top performer and became the parent of all commercial strains.
claims.episode_span: those strains produced several times more penicillin per gram of sugar consumed once they were grown under submerged conditions
claims.source_title: The Enduring Mystery of "Moldy Mary" - Tellus, USDA ARS
claims.supporting_quote: its penicillin yields under the submerged culture conditions required for industrial scale-up by pharmaceutical companies fell short of practical wartime production needs. A hardier, higher-yielding penicillin strain was needed.

claims.claim: The USDA laboratory in Peoria, whose expertise was fermentation, designed the deep-tank fermentation techniques and found that corn-steep liquor - a by-product of corn starch - sharply increased penicillin yield.
claims.episode_span: corn steep liquor, a cheap by-product of wet-milling, supplied nitrogen and growth factors at commodity prices
claims.source_title: How was penicillin developed? | Science Museum
claims.supporting_quote: The lab in Peoria had an abundance of corn-steep liquor, a by-product of corn starch. They discovered that when added to the mould broth, the yield of penicillin increased exponentially.
